page: Amazon Web Services m4.xlarge is a general-purpose virtual machine instance based on the Xen hypervisor. It features an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor running at 2.4 GHz, delivering 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with hyperthreading enabled. The instance is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per vCPU. It does not include local storage or dedicated GPU hardware, relying instead on network-attached storage options. Network connectivity is configured with a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark evaluations place the m4.xlarge in the lower performance tiers. Both single-core and multi-core CPU tests, including stress-ng and Geekbench, rank in the bottom 25% of tested hardware. Memory bandwidth benchmarks, such as uncached large-block reads and writes, also fall into the bottom 25% category, with read speeds at 24.01 GB/sec and write speeds at 21.65 GB/sec. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and Redis SET operations show lower relative efficiency, falling into the bottom 10% performance bracket.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m4.xlarge offers a balanced resource profile for legacy workloads that do not require high-performance compute or high-speed local storage. Given its dedicated CPU allocation and 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio, it is suitable for moderate general-purpose tasks. Recommended workloads include basic web serving, small-scale database operations, and lightweight background utility processing where predictable resource allocation is preferred over raw processing speed.
description: Amazon Web Services m4.xlarge is a general-purpose instance featuring 4 vCPUs and 16.0 GB of RAM, powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 processor running at 2.4 GHz. Built on the Xen hypervisor, this x86_64 instance provides a dedicated CPU allocation with a balanced 4.0 GB of memory per core. It does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and it operates with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. Performance benchmarks, including stress-ng, Geekbench, and memory bandwidth tests, consistently position this instance in the bottom 25% tier, with certain workloads like Redis SET operations falling into the bottom 10%. Consequently, the m4.xlarge is best suited for legacy general-purpose workloads, basic web serving, and lightweight background tasks that require a stable, non-burstable resource profile without demanding high-performance compute or fast local storage.
